snippet.title: How Women's Maximum-Security Prisons Actually Work | How Crime Works | Insider
snippet.description:
Jacqueline Montanez, formerly known as "Loca D," served 31 years in maximum-security women's prisons in Illinois and Florida.

She was originally sentenced to life in prison as a minor for double murders that she committed at age 15 for the Maniac Latin Disciples, a Chicago gang. Her sentence was later reduced to 63 years after a Supreme Court ruling on life sentences for minors was applied retroactively.

Montanez talks to Business Insider about security, dynamics between prisoners and guards, and gang relationships in women's prisons. She also reveals the details of gang violence, prison economies, pregnancy, and how prisoners navigate romantic relationships.

Since her release in 2022, Montanez has been an advocate for prison reform and has worked with several youth advocacy groups, such as Queens for Queens.

snippet.title: The Forgotten Gang That Ran New York — Before the Mafia
snippet.description:
Step into the dark, violent world of turn-of-the-century New York as we uncover the brutal true story of the Gopher Gang. From the squalid, crime-ridden streets and hidden basements of Hell's Kitchen, this Irish-American street gang terrorized Manhattan for decades, transforming from petty criminals into sophisticated architects of organized crime.

In this video, we dive deep into the lives of their most infamous figures:
-One Lung Curran: The consumptive but audacious leader who humiliated the NYPD with his infamous "cop-shucking" uniform stunts.
Battle Annie Walsh: The fearsome commander of the "Lady Gophers," whose brick-wielding shock troops famously routed the NYPD during brutal labor strikes.
-Owney "The Killer" Madden: The teenage enforcer who survived six bullets, delivered the legendary line "I'm doing my own dying," and then used his time in prison to transform himself from a street thug into a Prohibition-era kingpin and owner of the iconic Cotton Club.
Discover how the Gophers battled the rival Hudson Dusters, how "Happy -Jack" Mulraney's permanent grin concealed a killer's heart, and how the chaotic violence of Battle Row paved the way for the rise of the modern mob. This isn't just a gang story; it's a critical chapter in American criminal history, showing how poverty, brutality, and evolving criminal enterprise shaped a city.

snippet.title: Joe Masseria: The Mafia King Who Ruled Before the Five Families | Gangster Sleep Story
snippet.description:
Giuseppe “Joe the Boss” Masseria, born in 1886 in Marsala, Sicily, rose from the crowded streets of New York’s Lower East Side to become the first true Boss of Bosses in American Mafia history. Before the Five Families, before the Commission, there was Masseria — a man whose iron grip and ruthless ambition shaped the foundation of organized crime in America.

Arriving in the United States as an immigrant laborer, Masseria quickly adapted to the violent rhythm of early Mafia life. By the 1920s, he controlled gambling, extortion, and bootlegging across Manhattan, uniting fragmented Sicilian gangs under his rule. Known for his thick Sicilian accent, heavy appetite, and unshakable confidence, “Joe the Boss” turned the chaos of Prohibition into profit — and made himself the most feared figure in New York’s underworld.

But Masseria’s empire was not built on peace. His arrogance and hunger for control sparked the Castellammarese War, a bloody conflict that pitted him against a rising rival — Salvatore Maranzano. The war would consume the underworld for years, claiming dozens of lives and reshaping the Mafia forever.
In 1931, during a quiet lunch at Coney Island, Masseria’s reign came to an end — betrayed by his own men, including a young Charles “Lucky” Luciano, who would go on to rebuild the Mafia under a new order: the Five Families.

Frazier also reveals the most important attributes for fugitive recovery agents, how he survives multi-day stakeouts, and his deescalation techniques. In 2024 Frazier was shot in the chest while attempting to make an arrest. Despite undergoing numerous surgeries and spending several months in the hospital, he returned to bounty hunting in 2025.

Frazier has filmed himself operating and has created six seasons of "Bounty Tank," a reality show that is streaming on YouTube and Tubi. His documentary about his recovery, "BARS: Blessings After Real Scars," released in April.

snippet.title: How US Marine Special Operations Actually Work | Authorized Account | Insider
snippet.description:
Nick Jones is a former US Marine Raider who served in MARSOC, the Marine Corps’ elite special operations unit.

After starting his career as an infantry mortarman and scout sniper, Jones went on to complete the rigorous Marine Raider training and deployed multiple times to Iraq and Jordan. In 2020, Jones was awarded the Navy Cross for his actions during a chaotic firefight with ISIS fighters in northern Iraq in which he repeatedly charged into enemy fire to rescue wounded teammates despite being shot in the leg himself.

Jones speaks with Business Insider about Marine Raider selection, advanced infantry tactics, and operating alongside allied forces. He goes into detail about the intense realities of close-quarters combat and the firefight that led to his Navy Cross. Jones also reveals the mental and physical toll of combat, detailing his personal struggles with trauma, injury recovery, and alcoholism.

Following his retirement from active service, Jones has dedicated his career to supporting the veteran community. He is the founder of the Talons Reach Foundation, a nonprofit based in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.
